overview.body:
**Gná** (*gna*) ​— Messenger ‌of Frigg ‌· the Swift-Riding ​Goddess — ​belongs to ​the Norse tradition, ​where she ​is catalogued under ‌the domain ​"Messenger of ​Frigg". The name ‌means "To ​project, to ‌gaze".[^1]

Gná is ​one of ‌the handmaids ​of [[frigg|Frigg]], the ​highest goddess ​of the Norse ​pantheon, and ​serves as ‌her messenger. In ​the Prose ‌Edda, Snorri ​gives her a ‌brief but ​vivid chapter: ‌she rides the ​horse Hofvarpnir, ‌which can run ​through air ​and over ‌water, and carries ‌Frigg's errands ‌across the ​worlds. When she ​once encountered ‌a farmer ​building a fence ​in her ‌path, she asked ​why he ​worked so ‌hard; after he ​explained his ‌poverty, she ​arranged a marriage ​that made ​him wealthy. ​This small story ‌gives her ‌a gracious, aristocratic ​character — ‌the divine ​lady who notices ​mortal labor ‌and rewards ‌it.[^2]

PuniCodex restores ‌the name ‌as **Gná** ​and serves its ‌temple at ​[gná.com](https://punicodex.com/gna/). The restoration ​preserves the ​acute accent ‌on the final ​a that ​the ASCII ​form loses, and ‌exactly one ​historically valid ​Unicode restoration exists, ​which places ‌the name in ​Tier 1. ‌The plain ​ASCII form *gna* ‌survives as ​a modern ‌convenience imposed by ‌the early ​domain-name system; ​the restoration, not ​the fallback, ​is the form ‌the project ‌defends as ​philologically complete.[^1]

sources.citation: Snorri Sturluson, Prose Edda, Gylfaginning 35 / Skáldskaparmál, trans. Anthony Faulkes, Everyman / Viking Society for Northern Research, 1220.
Cleasby, Richard, and Guðbrandur Vigfússon, An Icelandic-English Dictionary, 2nd ed. (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1957), s.v. Gná.
Lindow, John, Norse Mythology: A Guide to the Gods, Heroes, Rituals, and Beliefs (Oxford University Press, 2001), s.v. Gná.

the-name.body:
The ​name is ‌attested in ‌Old Norse ​as **Gná**. ​Etymologically ​it means ​"To project, ​to gaze"[^1]. ‌The ​verb *gnæfa* ​means 'to ‌stand out, ​to tower, ‌to ​project'; related ‌forms suggest ​the idea ​of something ​raised ​or visible ​from a ‌distance. The ​name ‌may therefore ​evoke the ‌messenger who ​stands out ‌against ​the sky ‌or the ​gaze that ​reaches ‌far.[^2]

The ‌ASCII form ‌*gna* survives ​only because ​the ‌early domain-name ​system could ​not carry ‌diacritics; it ​is ​a technological ‌compromise, not ​an ancient ‌spelling. ​The Unicode ​restoration **Gná** ​recovers the ​acute accent ‌of ‌the original ​directly in ‌the address ​bar. The ​original ‌carries stress, ‌and exactly ‌one historically ‌valid ​Unicode restoration ‌exists, which ​places the ​name in ​Tier ‌1.

The ​letter-by-letter transformation ​runs:

- ​**g** ‌→ **G** ​— Same, ​capitalized
- ​**n** → ‌**n** ​— Same
‌- **a** ​→ **á** ‌— A ​with ‌acute: stressed ‌a

The ​project holds ​the ​domain **gná.com** ​as the ‌canonical home ‌of this ​name.[^1]

sources.citation: Snorri Sturluson, Prose Edda, Gylfaginning 35 / Skáldskaparmál, trans. Faulkes.
Cleasby & Vigfússon, An Icelandic-English Dictionary, 2nd ed., s.v. Gná.

pronunciation.body:
The ​reconstructed ‌pronunciation ‌of the ​name ​is ​**/gnaː/** ​— ​Old Norse ‌Reconstruction.[^1]

​Phoneme ​by ‌phoneme:

​- ‌**G-** — ​Voiced ‌velar ​stop ​[g]
​- **-n-** ​— ​Alveolar ‌nasal ​[n]
‌- ​**-á** — ‌Long ​open ‌back ​[aː] ‌with acute ​stress ​on ‌the ‌final ‌syllable

​For the ​modern ‌speaker, ​the ​closest ‌approximation is: ​'GNAH' ​— ‌one ​syllable, ‌with ​a long, ​stressed ​'ah'.

​Kindred ‌and ‌historical forms ​of ‌the ​name:

​- ‌**Old ‌Norse** — ‌Gná, ‌messenger ​of ‌Frigg
​- **Modern ​Icelandic** ​— ‌Gná, ​unchanged

​Gná ​is Tier ‌1 ​because ​the ​Norse ‌form preserves ​the ‌acute ​stress ‌that ​ASCII ‌loses. The ‌restoration ​keeps ​that ​accent ​visible in ‌the ‌domain ​name.[^2]

sources.citation: Gordon, E. V., An Introduction to Old Norse, 2nd ed. rev. A. R. Taylor (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1957), phonology and grammar.
Cleasby & Vigfússon, An Icelandic-English Dictionary, 2nd ed.

original-script.body:
The ​name ‌is preserved ‌in ​medieval ​Icelandic manuscripts ​in ​the ​Latin alphabet ‌as ​**Gná** ​— Old ‌Norse ​(North ‌Germanic), attested ​13th–14th ‌c. ​CE in ​the ​codices ​of Snorri's ​Edda, ‌recording ​material centuries ‌older.[^1] ​Before ‌the Latin ​bookhand, ‌Old ​Norse names ‌were ​carved ​in the ‌Younger ‌Futhark; ‌no runic ​attestation ​of ‌this name ​survives.

​The ‌scholarly rendering ​proceeds ​step ‌by step:

​- ‌The ​normalized Old ​Norse ​spelling ​uses á ‌(a ‌with ​acute) for ‌the ​long ​stressed vowel.
‌- ‌In ‌the Younger ‌Futhark ​the ‌name would ​have ​been ​carved approximately ‌ᚴᚾᛅ, ​with ​the ᚴ-rune ​covering ‌both ​g and ​k ​sounds.
‌- The ​Unicode ‌form ​**Gná** is ‌a ​scholarly ‌normalization that ‌distinguishes ​the ​stressed long ​vowel ​from ‌the plain ‌ASCII ​form.[^2]

sources.citation: Snorri Sturluson, Prose Edda, Gylfaginning 35 / Skáldskaparmál, trans. Faulkes.
Gordon, E. V., An Introduction to Old Norse, 2nd ed. rev. Taylor.

domains.body:
**Gná** ​belongs ‌to the ‌Norse ​tradition ​as ​the messenger ​and ​attendant ‌of ​Frigg. Her ​domain ‌is ​travel, ‌communication, ​and the ‌gracious ​exercise ​of ​divine power ​on ​behalf ‌of ​the highest ‌goddess.[^1]

​### ‌Messenger ​of Frigg

‌She ​carries ‌the ​queen of ​the ‌gods' ‌errands ‌across ​the worlds, ​riding ‌a ​horse ​that can ‌traverse ​air ​and ‌sea.

### ​Swift ‌Travel

​Her ​horse Hofvarpnir ​embodies ​the ‌speed ‌and freedom ​of ‌the ​divine ​messenger.

‌### Patroness ‌of ‌Prosperity

‌The ​story of ‌the ​farmer ​shows ​her power ‌to ​transform ​mortal ​fortune through ‌a ​single ​intervention.

​### The ‌Watchful ​Gaze

‌Her ​etymology ‌suggests projection ​and ‌visibility ‌— ​the messenger ​who ​sees ​and ‌is seen ‌from ​afar.[^2]

mythology.body:
Gná's mythology ​is brief ‌but distinctive. Unlike ‌the more prominent ​goddesses, she ​has no eddic ​poem of ​her own; her ​story survives in ‌a short ​prose passage in ​Snorri's Prose ‌Edda.[^1]

### The ​Tale of ‌the Farmer (Gylfaginning ​35 / Skáldskaparmál)

‌Snorri tells ​how Gná was ​riding her ​horse Hofvarpnir on ​an errand for ​Frigg when ‌she came upon ​a farmer ‌building a fence ​in Denmark. She ‌asked why ​he toiled so ‌hard, and ​he replied that ‌he was poor ​and had ​no other way ‌to feed ‌himself. Gná then ‌arranged for ​him to marry ​a wealthy woman, ‌and from ​that union came ​a prosperous ‌line. The story ​is one of ​the few ‌in Norse myth ​in which ‌a goddess intervenes ​directly to improve ​a mortal's ​social condition, and ​it gives ‌Gná a character ‌of refined benevolence.[^2]

​### Hofvarpnir's ‌Parentage

Snorri adds ​the detail ​that Hofvarpnir was ‌born when ‌the horse Hrimfaxi, ‌which draws Night ‌across the ​sky, was bitten ‌by a ​fly — a ​typically learned etymological ​aside. The ‌horse's ability to ​run through ​air and over ​water makes Gná ‌a figure ​who crosses boundaries ​with ease.[^3]

​### Among Frigg's ‌Handmaids

Gná is ​listed alongside ‌Frigg's other attendants, ​including Fulla, ‌Hlín, and Sága. ​These figures ‌form a courtly ‌retinue around the ​highest goddess, ​each with a ​specialized function. ​Gná's function is ‌movement: she is ‌the one ​sent out.[^4]
